metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Liquid-cooled AI racks exceed the structural weight limits most data centers were built to support, making buildings rather than electrical capacity the bottleneck in retrofit projects more often than expected.

Traditional enterprise data centers were engineered around air-cooled servers weighing far less than today's liquid-cooled AI infrastructure. A modern AI rack with coolant loops, manifolds, and batteries concentrates weight that raises floors and concrete slabs were not designed to carry. When a retrofit project discovers it cannot add more racks without structural failure, no amount of additional power capacity solves the problem. The building itself becomes the constraint.

This matters because it resets how operators think about capacity expansion. A facility with available electrical power and cooling capacity cannot simply install more racks if the floor loading limit is already reached. Structural reinforcement is expensive, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible in existing buildings. The practical density of AI infrastructure in legacy data centers is therefore set by building engineering, not by the electrical infrastructure most operators focus on when planning upgrades.

This metric does not measure the cost or timeline of reinforcement, nor does it address new construction, where floor loading can be engineered to spec from the start. It also does not capture how common this constraint actually is across the installed base of data centers globally, only that it happens frequently enough to surprise the industry.
